title: The Red Tide of 1892 and the Oysters Left on Ojima
dek: Two years into his pearl experiments, a red tide killed most of Kokichi Mikimoto's oysters; the survivors on a small island gave him his first cultured pearls.

story.event: Losing most of his experimental pearl oysters to a red tide in Ago Bay and carrying on with the survivors on Ojima
story.summary: In 1892, about two years into Kokichi Mikimoto's attempts to culture pearls in Ago Bay, a red tide killed most of his oysters, leaving a smaller stock on Ojima island. He kept experimenting, and in July 1893 hemispherical cultured pearls were found in oysters there. He patented his method in 1896 and sold a first, small crop at the end of 1898.
paragraphs: In 1890 Kokichi Mikimoto, a pearl dealer from Toba and the son of a noodle-restaurant owner, took live pearl oysters to the Third National Industrial Exhibition in Tokyo. There he met Professor Mitsukuri, a zoologist at the Imperial University, who suggested oysters might be stimulated to make pearls. Mikimoto had been farming oysters in Ago Bay since 1888. He went home and began experimenting, on the inlet of Shinmeiura and on the small island of Ojima. His firm's 1907 booklet recalled that friends laughed at him for "throwing his money into the sea."

Natural pearls formed only by accident, and Ago Bay's harvest was thinning under heavy demand. For about two years he tried one method after another, advised by Mitsukuri and another scientist, Dr Kishinoue. Then, in 1892, a bloom of algae discoloured the water of Ago Bay and killed most of his oysters. According to Japan's national tourism agency, what remained was a smaller stock on Ojima. His firm later called this "red current" perhaps the most dreaded danger of all: it could "undo in one day the work of years."

He kept going with what was left, "trying all sorts of experiments and changing his methods from time to time," as the 1907 booklet put it. On 11 July 1893, a date now kept in Japan as Pearl Memorial Day, he and his wife Ume found hemispherical pearls grown against the inside of shells from Ojima; the tourism agency counts five. They were not round, but the agency calls them the first successfully cultivated pearls in the world. A government medal citation of 1906, reprinted in the booklet, summed up the early years plainly: his first experiments had been "only a series of failures."

He patented his method in 1896, began farming on a large scale at Tatokujima in Ago Bay, and sold a first, small crop at the end of 1898; a shop in Tokyo's Ginza followed in 1899. Perfectly round pearls came later, and the credit is shared: the tourism agency gives the first success to two other researchers, Mise Tatsuhei and Nishikawa Tokichi, whose method Mikimoto bought and refined. Red tides never went away; in the early years, his island museum notes, ama divers moved the shellfish to safety when they came.

quote.text: human power is extremely limited, and is infinitely surpassed by the power of external causes; we have not, therefore, an absolute power of shaping to our use those things which are without us.
quote.source_title: Ethics, tr. R. H. M. Elwes, Project Gutenberg eBook #3800
quote.connection: Mikimoto's venture was an attempt to shape something outside himself, persuading oysters to do on purpose what they otherwise did by accident. Spinoza names the limit he met in 1892. The story adds what the limit did not decide: what he did with the oysters that remained.

reflection: A red tide is not a judgement on the farmer. Mikimoto had done nothing wrong in 1892; the water changed, and years of work died in it. What he still had was a smaller stock on a small island, and the choice of whether to keep tending it.

Some of what goes wrong in your weeks is like that: a delivery that does not come, a meeting cancelled at the last minute, a body that insists on a day off. It helps to separate those from the things you could have done differently, because they ask for different responses. One asks for a lesson. The other asks only that you notice what survived, and look after it.
invitation: Think of one setback this month that came from outside your control. Write down one thing it left intact, however small, and give that thing ten unhurried minutes today.

cross_checks.claim: In 1892 a red tide killed most of Mikimoto's pearl oysters.
Hemispherical cultured pearls were found in July 1893 (11 July in two accounts).
The round-pearl technique was developed by Mise Tatsuhei and Nishikawa Tokichi and adopted by Mikimoto.

research_notes: Episode changed from the slate. The slate named a 1905 red tide (in which, by later popular accounts, about 850,000 oysters died and Mikimoto found round pearls among the dead). That version appears only on dealer and magazine pages and, apparently, in Robert Eunson's 1955 biography The Pearl King, which is not readable online; Mikimoto's own booklets of 1907 and 1911 mention red tides only in general terms and say nothing of a 1905 disaster. The 1892 red tide is documented by Japan's tourism agency and by Precious.jp, so this edition tells that one. Sources disagree on several details. Start date: the tourism agency says pearl-farming attempts began at Shinmeiura in 1888; Precious.jp says he began farming oysters in 1888 and then turned to pearls; the 1907 booklet says the idea came from Professor Mitsukuri at the 1890 exhibition. The story says he had farmed oysters since 1888 and began pearl experiments after 1890. Location of the red tide: the tourism agency says Ago Bay, Precious.jp says Ise Bay; the story follows the agency. Cause: AFP (2019) describes his crop being destroyed by a 'bacterial virus'; the two Japanese sources say red tide, which the story uses. Who found the pearls: Precious.jp says Kokichi and Ume together, the tourism agency says he; the story says 'he and his wife Ume'. The figure of five pearls comes from the tourism agency alone and is attributed to it. The 11 July date is given by Lang Antiques and Precious.jp; Precious.jp notes that Pearl Memorial Day was never formally designated by any body, so the story says it is 'kept' rather than officially marked. Round pearls: Lang Antiques and AFP credit Mikimoto with a round pearl around 1905, while the tourism agency and GIA credit the bead technique to Mise and Nishikawa, whose rights Mikimoto bought; the story says the credit is shared. GIA describes the 1899 Ginza store as three years after 'the first culturing successes', counting from the 1896 patent rather than 1893. 'Bootstrapped' rests on Precious.jp's statement that he began with his own money; one dealer page mentions a loan, which could not be checked. The Japan Tourism Agency files are a PDF and a Word document that load but are not machine-readable by the checker; their texts were extracted and read in full. The Spinoza passage is from the Appendix to Part IV of the Ethics and is applied here by analogy.
